newsitem.title: USA: Chidambaram says world confident in Indian economy.
newsitem.headline: Chidambaram says world confident in Indian economy.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister Palaniappan Chidambaram said the international community seemed more secure about his country's prospects than domestic investors and India's private sector had to boost confidence.

Chidambaram, who travelled to New York after attending the IMF/World Bank meetings in Washington, said India's commercial banks should reduce their high real interest rates and the stock market should try to attract small domestic investors.
When inflation came down very sharply to about 4.25 percent, banks had not lowered nominal interest rates.

"These interest rates must be brought down not by allowing inflation to creep up, but by challenging banks to bring down nominal interest rates," Chidambaram said. "We hope that the bankers take the message."
The Indian government has done all it can to stimulate the stock market, which does not seem responsive to positive macroeconomic developments.
"I cannot see any fundamental weakness in the economy, yet the stock market remains sluggish," he said. "The stock market needs to reform itself so as to woo small investors back."
The government reported on Thursday that export growth slowed in August, but the minister said this should not slow overall economic growth.

"It does concern me that both imports and exports were down," Chidambaram told Reuters Financial Television on Friday. "But I don't think (lower exports) will necessarily contribute to a slowdown in economic activity."
If the government can keep the fiscal deficit down and bring it down again next year, everything thing else would fall into place.
He reiterated projections for a budget deficit of 5.0 percent of GDP this year, dropping to 4.0 percent in years ahead. Turning to the rupee, he told RFTV that the exchange rate was competitive.
"We've looked at the real effective exchange rate and it may have appreciated marginally, but on balance, the exchange rate is quite competitive.
India will not accept a return to inflation.
"We have to walk a tightrope between inflation and growth ...We cannot buy growth with inflation," he said.
Foreign investors seemed secure about India's economic prospects and welcomed the decision by Standard and Poor's to raise to positive its outlook on India's BB-plus foreign currency debt rating.
The government would try to achieve the three criteria S&P said were needed for an upgrade: improving tax revenues, containing state spending and restructuring state firms.
He called for lower public deficits for state governments and pointed to recent restrictions on borrowing and overdraft facilities.
"States do have large fiscal deficits, but states cannot create money," he said. "If we enforce these limits state deficits will come down." -- 212-859-1671
